docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
In this assignment, I built a functional 2D software rasterizer from scratch. I implemented the core graphics pipeline, starting with the basic mathematical foundation of rasterizing single-color triangles using edge equations. From there, I expanded the rasterizer to support affine transformations for manipulating SVG elements and implemented barycentric coordinates to smoothly interpolate colors across geometry. Finally, I integrated texture mapping alongside multiple antialiasing techniques—including supersampling, bilinear pixel filtering, and mipmap level sampling—to accurately render high-frequency textures and eliminate moiré patterns.

The most interesting lesson I learned was about software engineering. In Task 1, I eagerly implemented complex optimizations (incremental edge function updates and early loop exits) to make the basic bounding-box rasterizer as fast as possible. However, when I reached Task 2 and had to expand the pipeline to support supersampling, I realized that these early optimizations made adapting the code significantly more difficult. I learned that in future projects, a much better approach is to first establish a functioning baseline pipeline that handles all features correctly before diving into deep, complex algorithmic optimizations.

docs.title: Triangle Rasterization Algorithm
docs.text:
To rasterize triangles, I implemented a bounding box approach. First, I determine the bounding box of the triangle by finding the minimum and maximum x and y coordinates of the three vertices, clamping them to the screen resolutions. I then iterate through every pixel coordinate \((x, y)\) within this bounding box.

For each pixel, I calculate the center point \((x + 0.5, y + 0.5)\) and perform a point-in-triangle test. This is done using the three test functions derived from the cross-product of the triangle's edges. If the point lies on the correct side of all three half-planes (either all positive or all negative, depending on the winding order), the pixel is considered inside the triangle and is colored using fill_pixel.

\[ L_i = (P_{i+1}-P_i)\times (x-x_i,y-y_i) \]

docs.title: Efficiency Check
docs.text: My algorithm is no worse than one that checks each sample within the bounding box because it does exactly that: it restricts the search space to the rectangle defined by \([min\_x, max\_x] \times [min\_y, max\_y]\). It never checks pixels outside this range, ensuring the complexity is proportional to the area of the bounding box rather than the entire framebuffer.

docs.title: Extra Credit: Optimizations
docs.text:
I implemented two optimizations to improve rasterization speed beyond the simple bounding box check.

  1. Incremental Test Function \(L\) Updates: Instead of computing the full test function \(L_i(x,y)=-(x-X_i)dY_i+(y-Y_i)dX_i\) for every pixel, I calculate an initial value at the start of the loop. For each step in the inner loop (as x increases), I simply update \(L\) by adding \(-dY\). When moving to the next row (as y increases), I add \(dX\). This avoids performing time-consuming multiplication operations for every single pixel.
  2. Early Exit: Since a triangle is a convex shape, if we are iterating along a line and have already entered the triangle, the moment we step outside the triangle, we know we will not re-enter it on that same line. I added a flag entered; if a pixel fails the edge check and entered is true, I immediately break the inner loop.

docs.title: Performance Comparison
docs.text:
I tested these changes using test3.svg. The Early Exit provided the biggest speed boost.

Version Average Time (ms) Speedup Baseline (Naive Bounding Box) 10.341 1.0x Optimization 1 (Incremental Updates) 9.427 ~1.10x Optimization 2 (Early Exit) 6.870 ~1.51x

docs.title: Supersampling Algorithm and Data Structures
docs.text:
Supersampling is a technique used to reduce aliasing artifacts by rendering the image at a higher resolution and then downsampling it to the output resolution. This process averages the colors within a pixel, creating smoother transitions at edges.

To implement supersampling, I modified the rasterization pipeline to support a dynamically sized sample_buffer.

  1. Data Structure: I resized sample_buffer from width * height to width * height * sample_rate, since each pixel in the original image is represented by sample_rate sub-pixels.
  2. Rasterization (rasterize_triangle):
    • Instead of testing a single point at the center of each pixel \((x+0.5,y+0.5)\), I divided each pixel into a \(\sqrt{\text{sample_rate}}\times\sqrt{\text{sample_rate}}\) grid. I iterate through this sub-grid, checking if the center of each sub-pixel is inside the triangle. Then I store the color of the triangle in the specific index of sample_buffer corresponding to that sub-pixel.
    • To maintain the efficiency optimizations from Task 1, I applied the incremental test function updates to work on this sub-pixel grid. The step size for the test functions \((dX, dY)\) is scaled by \(1/\sqrt{\text{sample_rate}}\).
    • Also, for the “early exit” from Task 1, I organized the loops to iterate over the high-resolution sample_buffer. By treating the pixel \(y\) coordinate and the sub-pixel \(\text{sub}\_y\) index as a combined row iterator, I can still detect when the rasterizer leaves the triangle on a specific sub-pixel row. Once stepping out of the triangle, I immediately break the inner loop to skip the remaining empty space on that row.
  3. Resolve to Frame buffer (resolve_to_framebuffer): For every pixel in the final image, I iterate over its corresponding sample_rate sub-pixels in the sample_buffer. Then calculate the average color of these sub-pixels and write the result to the frame buffer.
  4. Updates to Other Functions:
    • set_sample_rate and set_framebuffer_target: Resize the sample_buffer whenever the window is resized or the sample rate changes.
    • fill_pixel: Fill all sub-pixels of a pixel with the same color, ensuring points and lines remain visible.

docs.title: Why Extra Memory is Needed
docs.text:
Is it possible to achieve the same results without more memory?

Yes, it is possible, but it comes with significant engineering tradeoffs.

The sample_buffer requires sample_rate times more memory than the frame buffer because rasterization happens per-triangle, not per-pixel. When we draw a triangle, we update specific sub-pixels. Later, a second triangle might overlap the first one, overwriting some of those sub-pixels. To correctly calculate the final average color, we must store the independent color value for every single sub-pixel until all triangles are drawn.

To avoid errors, we would need to perfectly resolve the depth order of all triangles before rasterization, and draw them from back to front (Painter's Algorithm). This approach trades memory for time, because sorting geometry and handling intersecting triangles are complex and time-consuming (potentially \(O(N \log N)\) or worse).

docs.title: Transform Matrices
docs.text:
To support the SVG transformation, I implemented the three standard 3x3 matrices for 2D affine transformations in homogeneous coordinates:

  1. Translate \((dx, dy)\): Moves a point \((x, y)\) to \((x+dx, y+dy)\)

    \[ T(dx, dy) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & dx \\ 0 & 1 & dy \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

  2. Scale \((sx, sy)\): Scales the geometry by \(sx\) in the \(x\)-axis and \(sy\) in the \(y\)-axis

    \[ S(sx, sy) = \begin{bmatrix} sx & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & sy & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

  3. Rotate \((\theta)\): Rotates a point counter-clockwise by \(\theta\) degrees around the origin

    \[ R(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta & 0 \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

docs.title: Coordinate Pipeline
docs.text:
The full coordinate transformation pipeline in the renderer is defined as:

\[ \mathbf{p}_{screen} = \mathbf{M}_{ndc\_to\_screen} \times \mathbf{M}_{svg\_to\_ndc} \times \mathbf{M}_{element\_transform} \times \mathbf{p}_{svg\_coords} \]

My modification specifically targets the \(\mathbf{M}_{ndc\_to\_screen}\) matrix. Originally, this matrix only handled scaling and centering to fit the normalized device coordinates (NDC) into the window resolution.

docs.title: Matrix Construction
docs.text:
To implement rotation, I added a function DrawRend::update_ndc_to_screen() to modify the ndc_to_screen matrix. First, I defined the base scaling matrix (\(M_{base}\)) as follows, where \(S = \min(W, H)\) is the scaling factor:

\[ M_{base} = \begin{bmatrix} S & 0 & \frac{W - S}{2} \\ 0 & S & \frac{H - S}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

I then constructed the final ndc_to_screen matrix by wrapping this base matrix with translation and rotation operations relative to the screen center \((cx, cy)\):

\[ M_{screen} = T(cx, cy) \times R(\alpha) \times T(-cx, -cy) \times M_{base} \]

Where \((cx, cy)\) is the center of the screen \((\text{width}/2, \text{height}/2)\) and \(\alpha\) is the current view angle.

  • \(M_{base}\): Maps NDC to the default screen position.
  • \(T(-cx, -cy)\): Moves the screen center to the origin \((0,0)\).
  • \(R(\alpha)\): Rotates the view by \(\alpha\) degrees.
  • \(T(cx, cy)\): Moves the origin back to the screen center.

This ensures the image rotates around the center of the window rather than the top-left corner. Below is the robot with the viewport rotated:

docs.title: Explaining Barycentric Coordinates
docs.text:
We often specify attributes—such as colors, texture coordinates, or normal vectors—only at the three vertices of a triangle. However, to render a solid shape, we need to obtain smoothly varying values for every single pixel across the triangle's surface. To achieve this smooth transition from the given vertex values, we use barycentric coordinates for interpolation.

Barycentric coordinates provide a coordinate system for defining the location of a point strictly relative to the vertices of a triangle. A point \(P\) inside a triangle with vertices \(A\), \(B\), and \(C\) is expressed as a weighted sum of those three vertices:

\[ P = \alpha A + \beta B + \gamma C \]

For the point to be valid inside the triangle, the weights must satisfy \(\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 1\), and \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma \ge 0\).

To understand this visually, we took color interpolation as an example. The triangle above has one pure red, one pure green, and one pure blue vertex. Barycentric coordinates act as proportional weights based on area. If a point \(P\) is very close to the red vertex, its corresponding weight will be close to \(1\), while the weights for green and blue will be close to \(0\), making that pixel predominantly red.

As moving across the surface, these weights shift proportionally, which allows us to smoothly interpolate the colors across the entire geometry, resulting in the smooth gradients seen in the image.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
The function rasterize_interpolated_color_triangle is based on the standard rasterize_triangle function, which calculates the exact barycentric weights for every sample point to blend the colors \(C_0\), \(C_1\), and \(C_2\).

The edge functions used for the point-in-triangle test directly map to the proportional areas needed for barycentric coordinates:

  • \(L_0 = (P_1-P_0)\times (x-x_0,y-y_0)\). The edge function for \(P_0 \rightarrow P_1\), which gives a value proportional to the area of the sub-triangle formed by \(P_0, P_1, P\). Since this sub-triangle is opposite to vertex \(P_2\). \(L_0\) represents the weight for \(P_2\) (\(\gamma\)).
  • \(L_1 = (P_2-P_1)\times(x-x_1,y-y_1)\). The edge function for \(P_1 \rightarrow P_2\), representing the area opposite to \(P_0\). This determines the weight for \(P_0\) (\(\alpha\)).
  • \(L_2 = (P_0-P_2)\times(x-x_2,y-y_2)\). The edge function for \(P_2 \rightarrow P_0\), representing the area opposite to \(P_1\). This determines the weight for \(P_1\) (\(\beta\)).

The final weights are normalized by the sum of all three edge functions:

\[ \alpha = \frac{L_1}{L_0 + L_1 + L_2},\beta = \frac{L_2}{L_0 + L_1 + L_2},\gamma = \frac{L_0}{L_0 + L_1 + L_2} \]

docs.title: Precision Issue
docs.text: After the first implementation, an artifact appeared: A white line would render along the shared edges of triangles. This was identified as a floating-point precision issue where accumulated values drifted, causing points exactly on the edge to evaluate as microscopic numbers and fail the boundary check. To fix this, the edge function accumulator variables were changed from float to double, and an EPSILON = 1e-6 tolerance was added to the boundary checks to ensure robust rasterization without dropping edge pixels.

docs.title: Explaining Pixel Sampling and Texture Mapping
docs.text: Texture mapping is the process of projecting a 2D image (texture) onto a 3D surface. Because screen pixels rarely map exactly 1-to-1 to texture pixels, we must perform pixel sampling to determine the correct color for a given screen pixel. This involves mapping screen-space coordinates \((x, y)\) back to normalized texture-space coordinates \((u, v)\) and fetching the color from the texture image at that location.

docs.title: Texture Mapping
docs.text:
To implement texture mapping in RasterizerImp::rasterize_textured_triangle, I reused the code in rasterize_interpolated_color_triangle with a few changes:

  • Barycentric Interpolation: For points inside the triangle, I compute their barycentric coordinates \((\alpha, \beta, \gamma)\) with the same algorithm.But instead of interpolate the given color values, I interpolated the \((u,v)\) coordinates: \((u,v)=\alpha(u_0,v_0)+\beta(u_0,v_0)+\gamma (u_2,v_2)\).
  • Texture Sampling: Using the interpolated \((u, v)\) coordinates, I sampled the texture color. Depending on the current pixel sampling method (psm), I called either tex.sample_nearest(u,v) or tex.sample_bilinear(u,v). The resulting color was then written to the sample_buffer.

docs.title: Sampling Methods
docs.text:
1. Nearest Neighbor Sampling (sample_nearest)

    Nearest sampling is the simplest and fastest approach. For any given \((u, v)\) coordinate, it simply finds the single closest texel in the texture space and uses its exact color.

    1. Scale the normalized uv coordinates by the texture's width and height.
    2. Use the floor function to get the nearest integer texel coordinates.
    3. Clamp the coordinates to width(height)-1 to ensure they don’t exceed the texture boundaries.

  2. Bilinear Sampling (sample_bilinear)

    Bilinear sampling smooths out the texture by considering the 4 closest texels around the sample point and computing a distance-weighted average of their colors.

    1. Map the UV coordinates to the texture space: Because texel colors are technically sampled at the center of each pixel (e.g., at \(0.5, 1.5, 2.5\)), directly finding the surrounding neighbors can be complex. To simplify the computation, we scale the \((u, v)\) coordinates by the texture's width and height, and then subtract \(0.5\). This shifts the coordinate system so we can easily use the floor function to find the texel.
    2. Apply the floor function to the shifted coordinates to get the top-left index \((s_0, t_0)\), and add \(1\) to get bottom-right index \((s_1, t_1)\).
    3. After clamping the indices to prevent out-of-bounds access, fetch the colors of the 4 texels \((u_{00},u_{10},u_{01},u_{11})\).
    4. Perform bilinear interpolation: \(u_0=\text{lerp}(x-s_0,u_{00},u_{10}),u_1=\text{lerp}(x-s_0,u_{01},u_{11}),f(x,y)=\text{lerp}(y-t_0,u_0,u_1)\)

docs.title: Result Screenshot
docs.text: The screenshots above are images of the test2.svg rendered under four different texture and pixel sampling settings. By zooming in using the pixel inspector, we can clearly observe how the sampling methods handle the texture details, especially along curved boundaries and high-frequency color transitions.

docs.title: Relative Differences:
docs.text:
• At 1 sample per pixel:
    • Nearest sampling produces a highly blocky and pixelated image, because it simply takes the color of the closest single texel. This leads to severe aliasing along the edges of the shapes in the texture.
    • Bilinear sampling smoothly interpolates between the surrounding texels. This effectively blurs the boundaries and the lines, creating continuous color gradients.
  • At 16 samples per pixel:
    • Both Nearest and Bilinear look smooth, and it is difficult to tell them apart at a glance.
    • Reason: When we perform supersampling anti-aliasing, the rasterizer is taking 16 independent point samples within a single screen pixel and averaging them. This process of taking 16 slightly offset "nearest" samples and averaging them effectively mimics the weighted neighborhood averaging that bilinear sampling does—except it is happening in screen space. Because the high sample rate already provides massive spatial smoothing, the additional localized smoothing from bilinear sampling becomes redundant, resulting in nearly identical visuals.

docs.title: When will there be a large difference?
docs.text:
A large visual difference between Nearest and Bilinear sampling primarily occurs under two conditions:

  1. Texture Magnification: When the texture resolution is lower than the screen resolution. In this case, a single texel maps to multiple screen pixels. Nearest sampling will render these texels as solid squares, whereas bilinear sampling will create smooth gradients between them.
  2. Low Screen Sampling Rate: As observed above, if supersampling is enabled, the anti-aliasing process smooths out the blocks. The difference is only highly visible when supersampling is turned off or set very low.

docs.title: Task 6: “Level sampling” with mipmaps for texture mapping
Explaining Level Sampling
docs.text:
Level sampling is an antialiasing technique used in texture mapping to solve the problem of minification—when a texture is applied to an object that appears much smaller on the screen than the texture's native resolution. Without level sampling, sampling a high-frequency texture across a small number of pixels leads to severe aliasing artifacts due to the Nyquist theorem (moiré patterns).

Level sampling addresses this by precomputing a pyramid of progressively downsampled versions of the texture called mipmaps. If a pixel covers a large area of the texture, we sample from a higher, lower-resolution mipmap level. This ensures that the texture frequency roughly matches the sampling frequency of the pixels, effectively acting as a low-pass filter to eliminate high-frequency noise.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
My implementation contains three main components: estimating the texture footprint, calculating the correct mipmap level, and executing the appropriate sampling strategy.

  1. Estimating the Texture Footprint (rasterize_textured_triangle)

    To determine how much texture space a single screen pixel covers, we need to calculate the rate of change of the texture coordinates \((u, v)\) with respect to the screen coordinates \((x, y)\). I achieved this by computing the barycentric coordinates for the current pixel \((x, y)\), and for its adjacent neighbors at \((x+1, y)\) and \((x, y+1)\).

    Using the linear property of edge functions, the edge function value \(L_i\) changes by a constant amount when stepping exactly \(1\) pixel horizontally or vertically (the optimization in Task 1.

    Using these updated edge functions, I calculated the new barycentric coordinates and the \((u, v)\) coordinates for the \((x+1, y)\) and \((x, y+1)\). These are passed to the sampling function as p_dx_uv and p_dy_uv within the SampleParams struct.

  2. Calculating the Mipmap Level (Texture::get_level)

    Once the texture coordinates for the current pixel and its neighbors are known, the finite differences can be used to approximate the partial derivatives:

    \[ \frac{du}{dx} \approx u(x+1,y) - u(x,y) \quad \quad \frac{dv}{dx} \approx v(x+1,y) - v(x,y) \] \[ \frac{du}{dy} \approx u(x,y+1) - u(x,y) \quad \quad \frac{dv}{dy} \approx v(x,y+1) - v(x,y) \]

    Because \((u, v)\) are normalized coordinates in the \([0, 1]\) range, I multiplied these differences by the texture's width and height to scale them into texel space.

    To ensure we don't alias in the direction of greatest stretch, I took the maximum of the lengths of the two difference vectors:

    \[ L = \max\left( \sqrt{\left(\frac{du}{dx}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{dv}{dx}\right)^2}, \sqrt{\left(\frac{du}{dy}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{dv}{dy}\right)^2} \right) \]

    Finally, the continuous mipmap level \(D\) is computed as:

    \[ D = \log_2(\max(L, 1.0)) \]

  3. Level Sampling Strategies (Texture::sample)

    The sample function acts as the core dispatcher, handling combinations of Level Sampling Methods (lsm) and Pixel Sampling Methods (psm):

    • L_ZERO: Ignores the computed level and samples from the base level 0 (full resolution).
    • L_NEAREST: Takes the continuous level \(D\), rounds it to the nearest integer, clamps it to the valid range \([0, \text{mipmap.size()} - 1]\), and samples from that discrete level.
    • L_LINEAR: Calculates \(D\), then bounds it between the adjacent lower and upper integer levels by using the function floor and ceil. It samples the color from both levels and performs a linear interpolation based on \(D\). When paired with P_LINEAR, this achieves full trilinear filtering.

docs.title: Visualizing Mipmap levels
docs.text:
To better illustrate the differences between these mipmap sampling methods, I used an LLM to generate a custom grid texture and applied it to a plane with extreme perspective distortion. The original provided images lacked the significant depth scaling required to clearly show mipmap transitions.

I also implemented a debug mode (toggled via the 'D' key) that maps the sampled mipmap level to a color gradient—ranging from blue (level 0) to red (highest level).

  • L_ZERO (Level 0 Only): As seen in the debug view, the entire plane is sampled at level 0 (blue). Looking at the texture render, the distant parts of the grid collapse into a aliased moiré pattern because the high-frequency grid lines cannot be represented by the sparse pixel sampling rate.
  • L_NEAREST (Nearest Level): The debug view shows discrete bands of color as the renderer switches from one integer mipmap level to the next. In the texture render, this causes noticeable sharp transitions in blurriness as the grid recedes into the distance.
  • L_LINEAR (Linear Level Interpolation): The debug view displays a perfectly smooth gradient from blue to red, indicating continuous transitions between levels. In the texture render, the sharp transitions are entirely eliminated.

docs.title: Tradeoffs: Speed, Memory, and Antialiasing Power
docs.text: Sampling Technique Configuration Avg. Render Time Buffer Memory Baseline L_ZERO, P_NEAREST, 1x SS ~14.1 ms 28,125 KB Pixel Sampling L_ZERO, P_LINEAR, 1x SS ~27.1 ms 28,125 KB Level Sampling (Nearest) L_NEAREST, P_NEAREST, 1x SS ~25.7 ms 28,125 KB Level Sampling (Linear) L_LINEAR, P_NEAREST, 1x SS ~37.2 ms 28,125 KB Supersampling (4x) L_ZERO, P_NEAREST, 4x SS ~53.1 ms 95,625 KB Supersampling (9x) L_ZERO, P_NEAREST, 9x SS ~115.5 ms 208,125 KB Supersampling (16x) L_ZERO, P_NEAREST, 16x SS ~201.3 ms 365,625 KB

docs.title: Speed
docs.text:
• Pixel Sampling: Switching from P_NEAREST to P_LINEAR roughly doubled the render time because it requires fetching four texels instead of one and performing 2D interpolation.
  • Level Sampling: Calculating the mipmap level adds overhead (although the mipmap pyramid is still generated during initialization, regardless of the sampling method). L_NEAREST increased time to 25.7 ms. L_LINEAR was the most expensive texture filtering method at 37.2 ms.
  • Supersampling: Render times scaled almost linearly with the sample rate. 16x supersampling caused the render time to increase to over 201 ms (a ~14x increase over the baseline).

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
• Pixel & Level Sampling: As shown in the data, the sample buffer memory remains constant at 28,125 KB regardless of the pixel or level sampling method. However, storing the mipmap pyramid itself inherently requires about 33% more texture memory than a single high-resolution texture.
  • Supersampling: Memory usage explodes as the sample rate increases. Moving from 1x to 16x supersampling increased the buffer memory from 28 MB to over 365 MB.

docs.title: Antialiasing Power
docs.text:
• Pixel Sampling: P_LINEAR effectively smooths out blocky textures when magnification happens, but fails to fix high-frequency noise and moiré patterns in minification.
  • Level Sampling: Mipmapping directly solves minification aliasing. By sampling from lower-resolution textures, it eliminates moiré patterns perfectly. However, it does not fix jagged polygon edges.
  • Supersampling: It fixes both texture aliasing and geometric edge jaggies, but at a massive cost to both speed and memory.

docs.title: Result Screenshot
docs.text:
The screenshots above are images of the checkerboard I generated.

  • L_ZERO and P_NEAREST: Without any filtering, this produces the worst result. The foreground pixels look blocky, while the distant parts of the grid collapse into moiré pattern.
  • L_ZERO and P_LINEAR: Bilinear pixel filtering smooths out the grid lines slightly in the foreground, making them look a bit softer. However, because it still strictly samples from the full-resolution texture, the distant moiré patterns remain completely unresolved.
  • L_NEAREST and P_NEAREST: By enabling nearest-level mipmapping, the distant moiré patterns are successfully eliminated. The grid fades into a gray blur in the distance. However, because we are using nearest logic on both the level and the pixels, we can clearly see sharp transitions horizontally across the image.
  • L_NEAREST and P_LINEAR: This combination eliminates the distance moiré while simultaneously softening the internal details of the grid within each level band. However, the sharp transition between the different mipmap levels are still visible. Only by upgrading to L_LINEAR would solve that problem.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
In this assignment, I built a system to work with and modify 3D surfaces. I started by implementing de Casteljau's algorithm to evaluate Bezier curves, and then extended it to render 3D Bezier patches. From there, I moved on to triangle meshes using the half-edge data structure. I began by calculating area-weighted vertex normals for smooth Phong shading. After that, I implemented basic local mesh operations—edge flips and edge splits—which became the stepping stones for the final part: mesh upsampling. By combining these local changes with vertex position updates, I successfully implemented Loop subdivision, along with extra features like boundary handling and the Modified Butterfly scheme.

The most interesting lesson I learned was the importance of drawing things out when working with complex data structures. When writing the code for edge flips and splits, the large number of half-edge pointer updates was pretty confusing at first. However, I found that by explicitly drawing out the "before" and "after" states of the triangles on scratch paper and carefully labeling every single vertex, edge, face, and half-edge, the logic became much clearer. Turning these drawings directly into code made sure I didn't lose track of any pointers, which helped the code work correctly on the first try and saved me hours of debugging.

docs.title: Part 1: Bezier Curves with 1D de Casteljau Subdivision
de Casteljau's Algorithm
docs.text:
Instead of calculating the complex polynomial equation directly, de Casteljau's Algorithm uses repeated linear interpolation to find a specific point on the curve for a given parameter \(t\), where \(t \in [0, 1]\).

We start with \(n\) initial control points: \(P_0, P_1, P_2, \dots, P_{n-1}\). For every two adjacent control points \(P_i\) and \(P_{i+1}\), we find a new point \(P'_i\) between them using the parameter \(t\). The mathematical formula for this is: \(P'_i = (1 - t)P_i + tP_{i+1}\)

After one full step of interpolation, we get a new set of \(n-1\) points. We repeat this exact same process on the new set of points.

Eventually, we stop the recursion when we are left with exactly one single point. This final point is guaranteed to lie on the Bezier curve at the specified parameter \(t\).

docs.title: Implementation Details
docs.text:
First, I implemented the helper function lerp(). The function simply takes two Vector2D points and the double t, and returns the newly interpolated Vector2D point \((1 - t)P_0 + tP_1\).

Next, I implemented the evaluateStep() function. This function is responsible for calculating one single recursive step of the algorithm.

  • It takes a std::vector<Vector2D> containing the current level's points, and returns a std::vector<Vector2D> to store the intermediate points.
  • I iterate through the given points, call lerp(points[i], points[i + 1], t) to interpolate between the current point and the next point, using the class member variable t. The resulting point is pushed into the result vector.
  • Finally, the function returns the result vector, which now contains one less point than the input vector, completing next level of subdivision.

docs.title: Part 2: Bezier Surfaces with Separable 1D de Casteljau
Extension of de Casteljau's Algorithm to Bezier Surfaces
docs.text:
We can solve the surface evaluation by separating it into multiple 1D operations. The inputs to this algorithm are an \(n \times n\) grid of original control points, denoted as \(P_{i,j}\), and two scalar parameters, \(u\) and \(v\).

  1. Row Evaluation (using parameter \(u\)): We first consider that each row of \(n\) control points, \(P_{i,0}, P_{i,1}, \dots, P_{i,n-1}\), defines a 1D Bezier curve parameterized by \(u\). Just as in Part1, we use the recursive linear interpolation step to evaluate the final, single point \(P_i\) on this specific curve at the parameter \(u\). We repeat this for all \(n\) rows.
  2. Column Evaluation (using parameter \(v\)): After evaluating all the rows, we obtain \(n\) new points: \(P_0, P_1, \dots, P_{n-1}\). These points define a new Bezier curve parameterized by \(v\). We again use the recursive step from Part1 on these points to evaluate the final point \(P\) at the parameter \(v\).

The point resulting from this final 1D evaluation is the precise point on the Bezier surface at \((u, v)\).

docs.title: Implementation Details
docs.text:
• lerp3D(p0, p1, t): This is the helper function. The function takes two Vector3D points and the double t, and returns the newly interpolated Vector3D point \((1 - t)P_0 + tP_1\).
  • evaluateStep(points, t): This function performs one level of subdivision for a given array of 3D points. It iterates through the points, calls lerp3D for every adjacent pair using parameter t, and returns a new vector containing \(n-1\) points.
  • evaluate1D(points, t): This function fully evaluates a 1D Bezier curve. It repeatedly calls evaluateStep() inside a loop until the vector is reduced to exactly one Vector3D point. It returns this final point, which acts as our \(P_i\) from the algorithm.
  • evaluate(u, v): This is the main function that handles the Bezier surface. For each row, I call evaluate1D(row, u). This evaluates that specific row using the parameter \(u\). I push the resulting point into temp_points. After the loop, temp_points contains the \(n\) evaluated points that form the column. I call evaluate1D(temp_points, v) to evaluate this final curve using the parameter \(v\). This directly returns the final 3D point \(P\) on the surface.

docs.title: Algorithm
docs.text:
To implement Phong shading, we need to calculate the area-weighted normal at each vertex. Phong shading uses vertex normals to smoothly interpolate lighting across the surface. To calculate the area-weighted normal for a specific vertex, we need to find the normals of all the triangles connected to that vertex, scale each face normal by the area of that face, add them all together, and finally normalize the result.

  1. We use the half-edge data structure to circulate around the given vertex. Starting from the vertex's half-edge, we access the adjacent faces using: h = h->twin()->next().
  2. For each valid, non-boundary face, we find the 3D positions of its three vertices using the half-edge pointers:
    • \(p_0\): The current vertex position (h->vertex()->position)
    • \(p_1\): The next vertex position (h->next()->vertex()->position)
    • \(p_2\): The third vertex position (h->next()->next()->vertex()->position)

  3. A normal vector is perpendicular to the face. We can find this by taking the cross product of two edge vectors on the face. Let the two edge vectors be: \(v_1 = p_1 - p_0\), \(v_2 = p_2 - p_0\).

    The cross product \(v_1 \times v_2\) gives us a vector perpendicular to the face. A useful property of the cross product is that its magnitude is exactly equal to twice the area of the triangle formed by \(v_1\) and \(v_2\).

    \[ N_{face\_weighted} = v_1 \times v_2 \]

    Because the magnitude is already proportional to the area, simply computing the cross product automatically gives us a normal vector that is weighted by the area of the face.

  4. We accumulate these area-weighted normals for all faces connected to the vertex: \(N_{sum} = \sum (N_{face\_weighted})\). Finally, we return the unit vector of this sum to get the final vertex normal: \(N = \frac{N_{sum}}{||N_{sum}||}\)

docs.title: Implementation Details
docs.text:
• Initialize a zero vector Vector3D n(0, 0, 0) to store the sum.
  • I use a constant half-edge iterator (HalfedgeCIter h = halfedge()) because the function is marked const.
  • Inside the loop, I check if the face is a boundary using !h->face()->isBoundary(). We ignore boundary faces because they do not represent real surface geometry in this context. For valid faces, I extract \(p_0, p_1, p_2\), calculate the cross product, and add it to n.
  • The loop continues until h circles back to the starting halfedge().
  • Finally, n.unit() is called to normalize the accumulated vector and return the result.

docs.title: Implementation Detail
docs.text:
The goal is to convert two adjacent triangles \((a, b, c)\) and \((c, b, d)\) sharing edge \((b, c)\) into a new pair of triangles \((a, d, c)\) and \((a, b, d)\) sharing the flipped edge \((a, d)\). Here’s a diagram showing the local neighborhood of the edge before and after the flip, with all variables labeled.

  1. I first check if the target edge e0 is a boundary edge using e0->isBoundary(). If true, the function returns e0 immediately and does nothing, since we cannot flip boundary edges.
  2. Before making any changes, I iterate through the mesh starting from e0's half-edge and use the next pointers to collect every single element in the two triangles. I gathered:
    • 6 inner half-edges: \(h_0\) to \(h_5\)
    • 4 outer twin half-edges: \(h_{1t}, h_{2t}, h_{4t}, h_{5t}\)
    • 4 vertices: \(a, b, c, d\)
    • 5 edges: The center edge \(e_0\) and four outer edges \(e_1\) to \(e_4\)
    • 2 faces: \(f_0\) and \(f_1\)

  3. Next, I reassigned the pointers to form the new geometry:

    • Face \(f_0\) becomes triangle \((a, d, c)\). Its new half-edge loop is: \(h_0(a \rightarrow d) \rightarrow h_5(d \rightarrow c) \rightarrow h_1(c \rightarrow a)\).
    • Face \(f_1\) becomes triangle \((d, a, b)\). Its new half-edge loop is: \(h_3(d \rightarrow a) \rightarrow h_2(a \rightarrow b) \rightarrow h_4(b \rightarrow d)\).

    I used the setNeighbors(next, twin, vertex, edge, face) function to update all 5 pointers for each of the 6 inner half-edges at once.

    Unchanged Elements: The twin pointers for \(h_1, h_2, h_4, h_5\) remain exactly the same, because their connections to the outside triangles are not affected by the local flip.

  4. Finally, to ensure total consistency, update every vertex, edge, and face pointers back to a valid half-edge that belongs to it.

docs.title: Implementation Tricks
docs.text:
For this part, I did not experience a difficult debugging journey. My main trick was doing all the work on scratch paper before typing any code.

By drawing out the two triangles(like the graph above), explicitly labeling every single half-edge, vertex, edge, and face with variable names, and mapping out their relationships before and after the flip, I avoided confusion. Translating this visual diagram into the setNeighbors calls made the code work correctly on the first try.

docs.title: Implementation Detail
docs.text: I implemented the edge split operation by tracking and reassigning pointers for all affected mesh elements. To manage the complexity, I first drew diagrams of the mesh before and after the split to label every vertex, edge, face, and half-edge.

docs.title: Non-Boundary Edge Split
docs.text:
1. Like Part4, I first iterate through the mesh starting from e0's half-edge and use the next pointers to collect every single element in the two triangles.
  2. In summary, the split operation creates \(1\) new vertex \(m\), \(3\) new edges, \(2\) new faces, and \(6\) new half-edges. The position of the new vertex \(m\) is set to the midpoint of the original edge: \(m = \frac{b + c}{2}\)
  3. After creating the new elements, I established four triangle loops by reassigning pointers:
    • Face \(f_0\): triangle \((b, m, a)\). Its half-edge loop is: \(h_0(b \rightarrow m) \rightarrow h_9(m \rightarrow a) \rightarrow h_2(a \rightarrow b)\).
    • Face \(f_1\): triangle \((m,b,d)\). Its half-edge loop is: \(h_3(m \rightarrow b) \rightarrow h_4(b \rightarrow d) \rightarrow h_{10}(d \rightarrow m)\)
    • Face \(f_2\): triangle \((m,c,a)\). Its half-edge loop is: \(h_6(m \rightarrow c) \rightarrow h_1(c \rightarrow a) \rightarrow h_8(a \rightarrow m)\)
    • Face \(f_3\): triangle \((c,m,d)\). Its half-edge loop is: \(h_7(c \rightarrow m) \rightarrow h_{11}(m \rightarrow d) \rightarrow h_5(d \rightarrow c)\)
  4. Finally, I updated the pointers for all \(5\) vertices, \(8\) edges, and \(4\) faces to ensure they pointed to a valid halfedge.

docs.title: Extra Credit: Boundary Edge Split
docs.text:
I also implemented support for splitting boundary edges. If an edge is on a boundary, only the non-boundary face is split into two triangles. The virtual boundary face is not split; instead, the new vertex \(m\) is simply inserted into the existing boundary loop.

Because we only split one triangle, this operation requires fewer new elements: \(1\) new vertex, \(1\) new face, \(2\) new edges, and \(4\) new half-edges.

The implementation is nearly identical to the non-boundary edge split, with a few key differences:

  • Finding the Boundary Predecessor: To insert the new vertex into the boundary loop, I needed the predecessor half-edge (h3_prev). Since halfedges do not have a prev pointer, I iterated around vertex \(c\) using h_it->twin()->next() until I found the halfedge whose twin is on the boundary.
  • New half-edge loops:
    • Face \(f_0\): triangle \((b, m, a)\). Its half-edge loop is: \(h_0(b \rightarrow m) \rightarrow h_9(m \rightarrow a) \rightarrow h_2(a \rightarrow b)\).
    • Face \(f_1\): triangle \((m,c,a)\). Its half-edge loop is: \(h_6(m \rightarrow c) \rightarrow h_1(c \rightarrow a) \rightarrow h_8(a \rightarrow m)\)
    • Boundary: \(h_{3-prev}(x→c) → h7(c→m) → h3(m→b) → h_{3-next}(b→y)\)

docs.text: My debugging journey was relatively smooth—I only encountered some basic errors, like typos.. I avoided major bugs by treating this part similarly to Part4. Before writing any code, I drew the "before" and "after" states of the triangles on scratch paper. I labeled every variable and mapped out the exact pointer relationships. Translating this physical diagram directly into code ensured that I did not lose track of any pointers.

docs.title: Part 6: Loop Subdivision for Mesh Upsampling
Implementation Detail
docs.text:
I implemented the Loop subdivision algorithm using the recommended process. The core idea is to pre-compute all new vertex positions on the original coarse mesh, perform edge splits and flips, and finally update the vertex positions.

  1. For every original vertex in the mesh, we calculate its new position using the Loop subdivision weighted average formula:

    \[ v_{new} = (1 - n \cdot u) \cdot v_{old} + u \cdot \sum v_{neighbor} \]

    Here, \(n\) is the degree of the vertex. The weighting factor \(u\) is defined as \(u = \frac{3}{16}\) if \(n = 3\), and \(u = \frac{3}{8n}\) for all other cases.

    I iterated through the neighborhood of each vertex using h = h->twin()->next(). During iteration, I accumulated the positions of the neighboring vertices and counted the degree. The result is stored in v->newPosition, and the vertex is flagged with v->isNew = false.

  2. For every original edge, we compute the position of the new vertex that will be inserted at its midpoint. We can identify the two endpoints of the edge (\(A\) and \(B\)) and the opposite vertices in the two adjacent triangles (\(C\) and \(D\)). The formula used is:

    \[ e_{new} = \frac{3}{8}(A + B) + \frac{1}{8}(C + D) \]

    This calculated position is temporarily stored in e->newPosition, and the edge is marked with e->isNew = false.

  3. To prevent the iterator from processing newly created edges, I first collected all original edges into a vector. Then, I iterated through this vector and called splitEdge() on each. The newly returned vertex \(m\) is marked as m->isNew = true, and its position is assigned the pre-computed e->newPosition.

    Finally, I traversed the four edges surrounding \(m\) to flag them: the two edges making up the original edge remain isNew = false, while the two cross edges connecting to the opposite old vertices are marked isNew = true.

  4. I iterated over all edges and flipped any edge that met two conditions: it must be a newly created edge (isNew == true), and it must connect one old vertex and one new vertex.

  5. Lastly, I iterated over all vertices in the new mesh and copied the data from newPosition to the position.

docs.title: Default Behavior
docs.text:
When Loop subdivision is applied to a cube, the sharp 90-degree corners and straight edges are heavily smoothed out. After several iterations, the cube loses its geometric sharpness entirely.

In the algorithm, each vertex's new position is calculated as a weighted average of its one-ring neighbors. For vertices at sharp corners, the weighted average forcefully pulls the corner vertex inward, collapsing the sharp feature.

docs.title: Preserving Sharpness via Pre-splitting:
docs.text:
To reduce this smoothing effect and preserve sharp corners, we can manually pre-split the edges surrounding the feature before applying subdivision.

In the first image, multiple edge splits were performed iteratively on the edges converging at a single front corner of the cube. When the weighted average is calculated, the corner vertex is only pulled toward these close neighbors rather than being pulled toward the distant center of the original faces. As a result, the pre-split corner successfully resists the smoothing effect and remains a sharp point. The rest of the unmodified cube smooths away.

docs.title: Cube Asymmetry
docs.text:
When loading default cube model and performing several iterations of Loop subdivision, the cube becomes slightly asymmetric. This happens because the starting topology of the cube is asymmetric.

Each square face is constructed using two triangles divided by a single diagonal edge. Loop subdivision updates vertex positions based on their vertex degree. Because these diagonals are oriented in a specific direction, vertices have uneven degrees, so the weighted average pulls the geometry more strongly along the direction of the diagonals.

docs.title: Pre-processing Solution:
docs.text:
To make the cube subdivide symmetrically, we need to make its initial topology symmetric. Before subdividing, I split the diagonal edge on every face of the cube so that each square face is made up of four symmetric triangles.

With this pre-processing, every corner vertex of the cube has the same degree. When Loop subdivision is applied, the weights are distributed evenly in all directions, causing the cube to smooth into a perfectly symmetric shape.

docs.title: Extra Credit: Supporting Meshes with Boundaries
docs.text: To support meshes with boundaries, the splits and flips operations remain identical, but the position calculations in Steps 1 and 2 require a different logic.

docs.title: Boundary Vertex Update
docs.text:
For old vertices on a boundary, the standard one-ring neighborhood formula would cause the boundary to shrink aggressively. Instead, we use a cubic B-spline rule. A boundary vertex connects to exactly two other boundary vertices (\(A\) and \(B\)). The new position is calculated as:

\[ v_{new} = \frac{1}{8}(A + B) + \frac{3}{4} \cdot v_{old} \]

docs.title: Boundary Edge Midpoint
docs.text:
For boundary edges, there are no opposite vertices \(C\) and \(D\) because the edge only borders a single interior triangle. Therefore, the new vertex position simply becomes the exact midpoint of the boundary edge:

\[ e_{new} = \frac{1}{2}(A + B) \]

docs.title: Result
docs.text: This ensures that the boundary curves smooth out naturally without collapsing inward.

docs.title: Extra Credit: Additional Subdivision Schemes-Modified Butterfly
docs.text:
The Modified Butterfly scheme is an interpolating scheme, whereas Loop is an approximating scheme. This means that in the Butterfly scheme, the positions of the original vertices are preserved.

The implementation is identical to Loop subdivision, but Steps 1 and 2 use different calculations.

docs.title: Original Vertex
docs.text: The Modified Butterfly implementation simply copies the original positions directly: v->newPosition = v->position.

docs.title: New Midpoint
docs.text:
The formula changes depending on the degree of the edge's endpoints:

  • Regular Edges: If both endpoints of an interior edge are regular (\(K = 6\)), we use the standard 8-point butterfly stencil. The new position is calculated using the endpoints \((p, q)\), the opposite vertices in the adjacent triangles \((c_1, c_2)\), and the four wing vertices \((w_1, w_2, w_3, w_4)\) that form the extended neighborhood:
\[ e_{new} = \frac{1}{2}(p + q) + \frac{1}{8}(c_1 + c_2) - \frac{1}{16}(w_1 + w_2 + w_3 + w_4) \]

  • Extraordinary Vertices: For an extraordinary vertex \(v\) (\(K \neq 6\)), we calculate a weighted sum of its 1-ring neighbors.

    • For \(K=3\): \(s_0 = \frac{5}{12}, \quad s_1 = s_2 = -\frac{1}{12}\)
    • For \(K=4\): \(s_0 = \frac{3}{8}, \quad s_1 = s_3 = 0, \quad s_2 = -\frac{1}{8}\)

    • For \(K \geq 5\), the weights are calculated using trigonometric functions:

      \[ s_j = \frac{1}{K} \left( \frac{1}{4} + \cos\left(\frac{2\pi j}{K}\right) + \frac{1}{2} \cos\left(\frac{4\pi j}{K}\right) \right) \]

    The new vertex position is then: \(\frac{3}{4} v + \sum s_j \cdot neighbor_j\).

  • Boundary Edges: For boundary edges, we use the two endpoints \((p, q)\) and their respective outer boundary neighbors \((a, d)\):

\[ e_{new} = -\frac{1}{16}a + \frac{9}{16}p + \frac{9}{16}q - \frac{1}{16}d \]

docs.title: Result
docs.text: Because the Modified Butterfly is an interpolating scheme, the mesh does not shrink inward the way it does with Loop subdivision. Instead, it bulges slightly outward between the original control points to create a smooth surface.

docs.title: Part 1: Ray Generation and Scene Intersection
Ray Generation and Pixel Sampling
docs.text:
The ray generation pipeline maps normalized 2D image coordinates to 3D world-space rays.

In Camera::generate_ray, we first calculate the size of the virtual camera sensor using the field of view angles: \(\text{halfW} = \tan(\frac{hFov}{2})\) and \(\text{halfH} = \tan(\frac{vFov}{2})\). We then linearly map the input normalized coordinates \((x, y)\) to the sensor plane coordinates \((cx, cy)\).

Because the camera looks down the \(-Z\) axis, the direction vector in camera space is \((cx, cy, -1)\). We normalize this vector. To transform this direction from camera space to world space, we multiply it by the camera-to-world rotation matrix c2w. Finally, we construct a Ray originating from the camera's position pos and set its valid intersection range using min_t = nClip and max_t = fClip to ignore objects outside the clipping planes.

In PathTracer::raytrace_pixel, we perform Monte Carlo integration to estimate the radiance of each pixel. We use gridSampler->get_sample() to generate ns_aa random sample points within the pixel area. For each sample, we generate a ray, calculate its radiance using est_radiance_global_illumination, and add it to a total sum. Finally, we divide the total sum by the number of samples to get the average radiance and update the pixel buffer.

docs.title: Triangle Intersection Algorithm
docs.text:
To implement the ray-triangle intersection, I used the Möller-Trumbore algorithm. This algorithm is highly efficient because it directly solves for the intersection point and the barycentric coordinates without needing to calculate the plane equation first.

The core of the algorithm combines the ray equation with the barycentric definition of a triangle:

\[ O+tD=(1-b_1-b_2)P_0+b_1P_1+b_2P_2 \]

Where \(O\) is the ray origin, \(D\) is the ray direction, \(t\) is the distance along the ray, and \(P_1, P_2, P_3\) are the triangle vertices.

By rearranging the terms and defining the edge vectors (\(E_1 = P_1 - P_0\), \(\vec{E}_2 = \vec{P}_2 - \vec{P}_0\)) and the distance from the ray origin to the first vertex (\(S = O - P_0\)), we construct a \(3 \times 3\) linear system: \([-D, E_1, E_2] [t, b_1, b_2]^T = S\).

Then, we solve this system for the unknowns (\(t\), \(b_1\), \(b_2\)) using Cramer's rule, which expresses the solution in terms of determinants.

\[ \begin{bmatrix} t \\ b_1 \\ b_2 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{\det(D, E_1, E_2)} \begin{bmatrix} \det(S, E_1, E_2) \\ \det(-D, S, E_2) \\ \det(-D, E_1, S) \end{bmatrix} \]

Finally, the determinants are rewritten using scalar triple products: \(\det(A, B, C) = A \cdot (B \times C) = - A \cdot (C \times B)\):

\[ \begin{bmatrix} t \\ b_1 \\ b_2 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{S_1 \cdot E_1} \begin{bmatrix} S_2 \cdot E_2 \\ S_1 \cdot S \\ S_2 \cdot D \end{bmatrix} \]

Where \(S_1 = D \times E_2, S_2 = S \times E_1\)

docs.title: BVH Construction Algorithm
docs.text:
In BVHAccel::construct_bvh, we use a recursive approach to build the bounding volume hierarchy. We first iterate from start to end to compute a bounding box (BBox) that includes all primitives in the current node. We then check the leaf node case: if the total number of primitives is less than or equal to max_leaf_size, we create a leaf node, assign the start and end iterators to it, and return the node.

If the node contains more primitives than max_leaf_size, we must split it to create an internal node. For our splitting heuristic, we use the average centroid along the longest axis. We first compute a centroid_bbox that bounds the centroids of all current primitives. We evaluate the extents of this centroid_bbox in the \(x\), \(y\), and \(z\) dimensions and select the longest one as our splitting axis.

Then, we calculate the splitting point by averaging the centroid positions of all primitives along this chosen axis.

Next, we use std::partition to divide the primitives based on the split point. Primitives with a centroid coordinate less than the split point are partitioned to the left side, and the rest to the right. To prevent infinite recursion in edge cases where all primitives cluster on one side (i.e., mid == start or mid == end), we explicitly force the array to split in the middle: mid = start + count / 2.

Finally, we recursively call construct_bvh to build the left (node->l) and right (node->r) child nodes.

docs.title: Performance Analysis
docs.text:
cow.dae CBcoil.dae CBbunny.dae CBdragon.dae

Implementing BVH acceleration provides massive performance improvements. Without a BVH tree, the ray tracer tests every ray against every primitive, resulting in \(O(N)\) time complexity per ray. By organizing primitives into a BVH tree, we reduce the intersection testing time complexity to roughly \(O(\log N)\).

Scene Name Render Time (No BVH) Render Time (With BVH) cow 6.3221s 0.0362s coil 7.9054s 0.0265s bunny 49.7231s 0.0266s dragon 165.0446s 0.0305s

As shown, scenes like the dragon that took over two minutes to render natively now complete in fractions of a second. This logarithmic efficiency becomes absolutely essential for rendering large models.

docs.title: Uniform Hemisphere Sampling
docs.text:
In PathTracer::estimate_direct_lighting_hemisphere, we use Monte Carlo integration to estimate the direct lighting by sampling uniformly over a hemisphere.

We loop num_samples times. In each iteration, we sample a random incoming direction \(w_{in}\) using hemisphereSampler->get_sample(). We convert this local direction to world space and create a sample ray starting from the hit point hit_p.

Then, We check if this ray intersects any object in the scene using the BVH. If it hits a light source, we get its emitted radiance. We calculate the light contribution using the reflection equation: \(f(w_{out}, w_{in}) \cdot L_i \cdot \cos(\theta) \cdot 2\pi\). The \(2\pi\) term comes from dividing by the probability density function of uniform hemisphere sampling, which is \(1 / 2\pi\).

Finally, we sum these values and divide by num_samples to get the average.

docs.title: Importance Sampling
docs.text:
In PathTracer::estimate_direct_lighting_importance, instead of sampling random directions, we directly sample the light sources.

We iterate through every light in scene->lights. For each light, we take ns_area_light samples (or just 1 sample if it is a point light). Then, we use light->sample_L to get the incoming radiance \(L_i\), the world direction to the light \(w_{i\_world}\), the distance to the light, and the \(\text{pdf}\).

We convert the direction to local space and check if the light is behind the surface (\(w_{i\_local}.z \le 0\)). If it is in front, we cast a shadow ray from hit_p towards the light. The max_t of the shadow ray is set to distToLight - EPS_F to avoid intersecting the light itself. If the shadow ray does not intersect anything in the BVH, the point is not in shadow. We then calculate the contribution using the formula: \(f(w_{out}, w_{i\_local}) \cdot L_i \cdot \frac{\cos(\theta)} {\text{pdf}}\).

Finally, we average the samples for each light and add them together to get the total direct lighting.

docs.title: Result
docs.text: CBbunny.dae(-H -s 64 -l 32) CBbunny.dae(-s 64 -l 32) CBspheres_lambertian.dae(-H -s 64 -l 32) CBspheres_lambertian.dae(-s 64 -l 32)

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Uniform hemisphere sampling shoots rays in random directions, meaning many rays will simply hit empty space or non-emitting objects instead of a light source. This wastes a lot of computational power and results in a highly noisy image. In contrast, lighting sampling directly targets the light sources, guaranteeing that every sampled direction points toward a light. The only reason a sample would not contribute to the lighting is if it is blocked by an object. Because of this targeted approach, importance sampling converges much faster and produces significantly less noise with the same number of samples.

docs.title: Soft Shadows Noise Levels Comparison
docs.text:
Below are the renderings of the CBspheres_lambertian.dae scene using importance sampling with 1 sample per pixel (-s 1) and varying numbers of light rays (-l):

-l 1 -l 4 -l 16 -l 64

When rendering with only 1 light ray, the soft shadows under the spheres are very noisy. As we increase the number of light rays to 4 and 16, the noise in the shadow regions significantly decreases. At 64 light rays, the soft shadows become very smooth and accurately show the gradual transition from light to dark.

docs.title: Indirect Lighting Function
docs.text:
The indirect lighting function, at_least_one_bounce_radiance, calculates the light that bounces multiple times before reaching the camera.

First, we convert the outgoing ray direction (-r.d) from world space coordinates to local space coordinates (w_out). We initialize the total outgoing light, L_out, to \((0, 0, 0)\). If isAccumBounces is true, or if the current ray depth is exactly 1, we calculate the direct lighting by calling one_bounce_radiance(r, isect) and add it to L_out. If the ray depth is 1 or less, we stop here and return L_out.

Next, to calculate the indirect light coming from the rest of the scene, we need to sample a new incoming direction. We call isect.bsdf->sample_f(w_out, &w_in, &pdf). This function gives us a random incoming direction w_in, returns the BSDF value \(f(w_{out}, w_{in})\), and evaluates the PDF for this sampled direction.

Russian Roulette: We set a probability, cpdf = 0.7. We call coin_flip(cpdf). If the coin flip returns false, we terminate the ray and simply return the current L_out. If it returns true, we continue to trace the bounce.

Then, we convert the sampled local direction w_in back to world space coordinates (w_in_world). Then, we create a new bounce_ray. We check if this new bounce_ray intersects with anything in the scene. If it hits an object, we recursively call at_least_one_bounce_radiance(bounce_ray, new_isect) to get the incoming indirect light, L_indirect.

Finally, we use the Monte Carlo estimator formula to calculate the contribution of this bounce and add it to L_out:

\[ L_{out} = L_{out} + \frac{L_{\text{indirect}} \cdot f \cdot \cos(\theta)}{\text{pdf} \cdot \text{cpdf}} \]

docs.title: 2nd and 3rd Bounces vs. Rasterization
docs.text:
In the 2nd bounce image, we can clearly see color bleeding. The colored walls reflect light onto the bunny. The black ceiling is now lit by light bouncing from the floor.

The 3rd bounce is much darker because surfaces absorb light energy. But it still adds soft light to the deep shadows.

Rasterization usually uses direct lighting and fake ambient light. This physical path tracing approach creates significantly higher quality and more realistic images, because it naturally simulates how light actually scatters and interacts with materials in the real world.

docs.title: Accumulated vs. Unaccumulated
docs.text: The unaccumulated views become progressively darker with each extra bounce since surfaces absorb energy at every interaction. The accumulated views become progressively brighter and softer as they sum up all these layers of light. The biggest visual jump in the accumulated renders happens between depth 1 and 2, where the black shadows are softened by the first layer of indirect light; subsequent depths add brightness and remove noise, which perfectly aligns with the fading energy we see in the higher-depth unaccumulated renders.

docs.title: Sample-Per-Pixel Rates
docs.text:
\(s=1\) \(s=2\) \(s=4\) \(s=8\) \(s=16\) \(s=64\) \(s=256\) \(s=1024\)

As the sample-per-pixel rate increases, the noise in the image drops significantly. At very low rates like 1, 2, and 4 spp, the image is extremely noisy because the Monte Carlo estimation has high variance. As we increase the number of samples, the variance decreases and the image converges to the true result.

By 64 spp, the image is much smoother, but noise is still visible in the shadows. At 256, 1024 spp, the noise is almost gone, giving us a clean render with smooth shadows and clear global illumination. This perfectly shows how adding more samples improves the accuracy of the Monte Carlo estimate.
